en: It tore the ears to pieces.
The champion beside him
Struck the war drum.
The drum was beaten hard;
His sorcerers and judges of men,
When they heard the war drum's sound,
Many lords surged up.
Across Esenkan's sandy square,
They walked in hurrying haste.
While his champion stood thus,
They ran in alarm and commotion,
Bending their knees to the ground.
His sorcerers, his judges of men,
His wonder-workers and diviners,
Whose fame made people tremble,
The sixty-page Burkan scripture
They had studied thoroughly.
When his judges of men arrived,
‘Examine this one,’ he said.
The people stood gathered;
He gave a stern command.
By Bilerik's neck
They fastened and bound him firmly.
Seven of his giants led him,
Driving him up and down.
His judges of men looked him over;
To hero Esenkan, the great khan,
They began to tell his nature:
“He is a lord and a lion;
This Burut who has fallen into our hands
Is an exceptionally fine hero.
To the blood-drinking, bloodthirsty Burut
He is one who will be a companion.
Of middling height and broad shoulders,
He is a hero who will break the Oirats;
At Kakanchyn's Beijing
He is a hero who will fire his shots.
Broad-chested, wide-breasted,
That imposing, wretched Burut—
What a day this has become!
Unless you secure his hands and feet
And keep him in humiliation,
Your heaped treasury wealth,
He is a son who will scatter it.
Without stopping, from the kakan
He is a son who will escape.
One day, his desire,
He is a son who will attain it.
If he breaks free, fleeing to his people,
He is a son who will depart.
His eyes are red, his face a live coal;
In many lands there is no such youth.
He is no slave who will remain idle,
No son who will stay in Beijing.
To your side is Kakanchyn,
Before you is Bakburchun.
Ulungtu, Kentun and Tungsha,
We have traveled through all these.
Revealing everything through livestock,
Roaming and examining,
We have seen many cities.
Among heroes we have seen none like him,
From of old we have known none like him.
His bravery is unlike others',
His strength as a champion is great.
Of middling height and broad shoulders,
That gouge-cursed one is an outstanding man.
Looking and judging his appearance,
He is a twelve-year-old boy.
Encountered from the unseen—
Beijing is no easy place;
On what day was this boy encountered?”
Before Esenkan,
Chong Ayar, khan of the judges of men,
Chong Ayar stood and said this,
Telling a marvel to those who understood:
“The hare that falls into one's hands—
Will one prosper who lets it go?
Esenkan, you were the great lord,
I was the knowing magician!
The Burut who has fallen into our hands,
Secure his hands and feet,
Drive him toward the pit.
Attend closely to my words;
Into the dungeon forty rope-lengths deep,
Take him and cast him in,
Keep him firmly locked away!
‘Bilerik has been captured,’
Send this news to the Buruts!
Will they not heed your demands?
Those flame-cursed Buruts,
Will they not give whatever land you wish?
Will they not gather their chiefs,
Saying, ‘I will get the child back alive,’
Will they not offer their livestock and people as tribute?
This child who lies here,
To rescue him,
Will they not heed what you say?
Alty-Shaar and Margalang,
Samarkand beyond them,
Kokand and Andizhan at their side,
Their cities from there to here,
Will they not give them as tribute?
Will they not heed your demands?
We shall unleash a terrible fury;
Of the daughter-damned Buruts,
How much wealth we shall take!
‘If you do not give it, I shall kill him,’
From the daughter-damned Buruts
Let us demand their khanate.
If they do not agree at first,
If they do not give what is demanded,
The child who has fallen into our hands,
Let us bind his hands and feet.
Beating him up and down,
Let us humiliate and kill him.
At the border of the enemy we have in mind,
Facing the Muslims,
Let us slaughter their fierce ones.
To exact tribute firmly,
To inflict torment firmly,
The hero, brave Alöökö,
In the city of Margalang
Let us raise him as khan.
The mother-damned Buruts,
Let us find a way to slaughter them!
Let us impose grievous oppression;
Finding the Buruts' weak point,
Let us take much of their wealth!”
When Chong Ayar had spoken,
When Esenkan heard this,
His people shouted in joy.
Holding a joyous feast,
All his people gathered.
He had wealth scattered,
He hurried his champions,
A copper cauldron with forty handles
He had hung before his throne.
‘God has granted my wish,’ he said,
‘The enemy I had my eye upon,
Ezkara has brought him bound,’ he said.
All his sorrow scattered,
All his cares were opened and cleared,
Devising a thought no man could find,
All the peoples of the world,
Esenkan gathered them.
May he be wiped away—he held a feast.
The copper cauldron with forty handles,
He kindled a fire and brought it to the boil.
An idol as large as a house,
Above the cauldron,
He had it hung dangling,
He had it tied up high.
Slaughtering forty oxen at once,
He had them put in whole.
Slaughtering forty pigs at once,
Slaughtering forty puppies at once,
Slaughtering forty cats at once,
He had them all put in together.
He devised a thought no man could find.
The bells were rung hard;
The many lords, seething,
His Torguts swarmed to the last.
In fear of Esenkan,
The idol made of bronze,
‘This is our god,’ they said,
And all bowed down together.
All the Manchus gathered;
The idol made of bronze,
‘This is God,’ they said, worshipping it.
The Manchus and many Sibe grew excited;
They feasted for seven days,
Making ready their festive entertainments,
They gathered the governors.
A warrior such as Alöökö,
In the city of Margalang,
They raised him as khan.
Through this, Alöökö
Became a man with a white yurt.
Poor Bilerik,
To the great dungeon forty rope-lengths deep,
They took him and cast him in.
Without killing him or letting him perish,
Esenkan, full of wrath,
Had these men taken there
And kept at the treasury's expense.
Without dying or perishing, Bilerik
Is alive to this very day, they say.
Neither dead nor living,
Aykozho's Bilerik,
His days are wretched, they say.
Lying in the pit, aching,
He burns with grief, I hear.
‘My saintly elder Koshoy,
When will he bring relief?’
He keeps this in mind, I hear.
Lion Manas, my little foal,
I have told you the tale.
There is grief and sorrow in my breast;
I have said it; hear it well!
My child, Manas, my little foal,
Your aged elder Koshoy is here.
Within your elder Koshoy
Is a lament no camel could carry!
The Chinese began the slaughter;
Those who so much as glanced back,
They slaughtered them.
My little foal, born bloodthirsty,
Listen to my words!
Souls flee at the sound of his voice;
Now Alöökö has become our khan!
If you truly are a lion,
The Kyrgyz who have gone astray,
Rescue them!
Ruling over Margalang,
His name has become Alöökö;
That swine Alöökö,
His strife has reached the world!
He was installed last autumn;
He slaughtered many and leveled them flat.
When he roars in anger,
Abandon hope against that unbeliever!
Those who answered him back,
Their two eyes, with cruel torment,
He gouged them out, I heard.
Those who refused to pay tribute,
Sprawling them like lean sheep,
He slaughtered them, I heard.
Dust rose from his passing;
That unbeliever Alöökö,
Souls fled at the sound of his voice.
An unbeliever with sixty sons, they say,
Who will not yield to all the world,
King Alöökö is a warrior, they say.
The glittering wealth of the world,
Alöökö keeps reaping it.
Taking tribute in gold,
Alöökö keeps sucking it dry.
Alöökö's might,
No mortal can reach it by boasting, they say.
A soul who says, ‘I will resist,’
Not one departs alive, they say.
Alöökö's wrath
Surpasses every man's, they say.
Binding a rope to the feet
Of a man who shows defiance,
He hoists him toward the sky, they say.
I have this dreadful thing to tell;
Alöökö's strife,
Lion Manas, hear it well!
Choosing camels from the pack animals,
He took them and inflicted humiliation, I heard.
Having them all beaten, leaving none,
He committed oppression, I heard.

Driving and beating the Sarts,
